UNPACKING MATH STANDARDS
Verify experimentally the properties of rotations, reflections, and 
translations: a. Lines are taken to lines, and line segments to line 
segments of the same length. b. Angles are taken to angles of the 
same measure. c. Parallel lines are taken to parallel lines.
What It Means to You
Students are able to visually identify rotations, reflections, and translations 
on two-dimensional figures, and to discern whether one figure can be 
taken to another by a combination of those transformations. Students 
will discover that these transformations are rigid motions that take line 
segments to line segments of the same length, angles to angles of the 
same measure, and parallel lines to parallel lines.
In particular, students will demonstrate an ability to graph 
transformations on the coordinate plane. They will perform rotations by 
multiples of 90 degrees clockwise or counterclockwise, translations by 
units vertically and horizontally, and reflections over the axes and other 
horizontal and vertical lines. Students will be able to describe the effect 
of these transformations using coordinates.

Using Mathematical Practices and Processes
Reason abstractly and quantitatively.  In this lesson, students will 
translate figures on a coordinate plane. They need to realize that 
the dimensions, angle measures, and relationships between sides 
do not change when a figure is translated. They will use this 
information to reason that these relationships do not change, 
regardless of the direction of the translation.

using coordinates.

figures using coordinates.
What It Means to You
Students  describe translations and their effects on figures in the 
mapping plane. They identify and represent translations using 
mapping notation, and they graph images of translations, given 
preimages and descriptions of the translation. They recognize what 
they experimentally verified in the previous lesson: that when a 
figure is translated, side lengths and angle measures remain the 
same, and parallel sides remain parallel. 
In later lessons, students will use what they have learned about 
translations on a coordinate plane to understand the concept of 
congruence.

What It Means to You
Students describe reflections and their effects on figures. First students 
perform these reflections given the preimages and the description of 
the reflection. Then they learn the effects on the image and its 
coordinates within a coordinate plane when reflecting the preimage. 
Once again, they learn that the image’s side lengths and angles remain 
the same as the preimage. The difference with reflections is that the 
image faces a different direction than the preimage.
